details:
**"Surprise" Symphony (No. 94 in G major)**
Haydn's most famous symphony, one of his London symphonies. Its Andante second movement opens with a soft theme on C-C-E-E-G-G-E, which is followed by a sudden fortissimo G major chord, supposedly meant to wake dozing listeners; in German it is called the "Paukenschlag" ("drumstroke") symphony. Haydn later quoted the theme in his oratorio The Seasons, where a plowman whistles it.

**"Farewell" Symphony (No. 45 in F-sharp minor)**
A Sturm und Drang symphony in the unusual key of F-sharp minor. In the finale the musicians stop playing one by one, snuff out the candles on their stands, and leave, until only two muted violins remain; it was a hint to Prince Nikolaus Esterházy that his musicians wanted to leave his summer palace at Eszterháza and go home to their families.

**"Father of the Symphony" and "Father of the String Quartet"**
Haydn's standard nicknames. He wrote 104 numbered symphonies (often counted as 106 with two unnumbered ones) and dozens of string quartets, works for two violins, viola, and cello, and he did more than anyone else to establish both genres in the Classical era.

**"Emperor" Quartet and "Gott erhalte Franz den Kaiser"**
Haydn wrote the anthem "Gott erhalte Franz den Kaiser" ("God Save Emperor Francis," lyrics by Lorenz Leopold Haschka) for Francis II and then used it as the theme of variations in the second movement of his "Emperor" Quartet. The melody, opening G-A-B-A-C-B, was later set to August Heinrich Hoffmann von Fallersleben's words as the "Deutschlandlied," the German national anthem.

**The Creation**
Haydn's oratorio (1798) based on the Book of Genesis and Milton's Paradise Lost. It opens with "The Representation of Chaos"; when the chorus sings "and there was light," it bursts into a fortissimo C major chord. The archangels Raphael, Uriel, and Gabriel narrate the six days of creation, Part I ends with the chorus "The Heavens Are Telling the Glory of God," and Adam and Eve appear as bass and soprano in Part III.

**Esterházy family**
The Hungarian princely family that employed Haydn as court musician (and later Kapellmeister) for decades, especially Prince Nikolaus "the Magnificent" at the palace of Eszterháza. He wrote his late masses, such as the "Nelson" Mass, for the Esterházys.

**London Symphonies**
Haydn's final twelve symphonies (Nos. 93–104), written for impresario Johann Peter Salomon during two visits to London in the 1790s. They include the "Surprise," "Miracle," "Military," "Clock," "Drumroll" (No. 103, which opens with a timpani roll), and "London" symphonies.

**"The Joke" Quartet (Op. 33 No. 2)**
A string quartet in E-flat major whose finale repeatedly fakes its ending with pauses, so the audience cannot tell when it has actually finished. It belongs to the six Op. 33 "Russian" quartets, dedicated to Grand Duke Paul of Russia, which inspired Mozart's six quartets dedicated to Haydn (including the "Hunt" and "Dissonance").

**Op. 76 "Erdődy" Quartets ("Fifths," "Emperor," "Sunrise")**
A set of six string quartets dedicated to Count Joseph Erdődy. The "Fifths" quartet opens with falling perfect fifths and contains a canonic "Witches' Minuet"; the set also includes the "Emperor" and the "Sunrise," named for its rising opening melody.

**"Miracle" Symphony**
The nickname of Symphony No. 96, from the story that a chandelier fell during its London premiere but injured no one because the audience had crowded toward the stage. The incident is now believed to have actually occurred at the premiere of Symphony No. 102.

**Masses (Nelson Mass, Mass in Time of War, Harmoniemesse)**
Haydn's late masses for the Esterházys include the "Nelson" Mass (Missa in Angustiis, "Mass for Troubled Times," originally scored without woodwinds), the "Mass in Time of War" (Paukenmesse, named for the timpani in its Agnus Dei), and his last major work, the B-flat major "Harmoniemesse," named for its large wind section.

**The Seven Last Words of Christ**
An orchestral work by Haydn of slow meditations on Christ's last words on the cross, ending with a fast "Earthquake" movement. Haydn also arranged it for string quartet and as an oratorio.

**Trumpet Concerto in E-flat major**
Haydn's concerto (1796) written for Anton Weidinger's newly invented keyed trumpet, which could play chromatic melodies in the low register. Johann Nepomuk Hummel also wrote a concerto for the same instrument.

**Other symphony nicknames ("Hornsignal," "Bear," "Philosopher," "Military," "Clock")**
No. 31 "Hornsignal" uses four horns, No. 82 "Bear" (a Paris symphony) has a droning, bagpipe-like finale, and No. 22 "Philosopher" uses two English horns instead of oboes. The "Military" (No. 100) imitates Turkish janissary music with percussion, and the "Clock" (No. 101) has a ticking accompaniment in its slow movement.

**Hoboken catalog**
The standard catalog of Haydn's works compiled by Dutch musicologist Anthony van Hoboken, so his works are identified with "Hob." numbers.
